messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Fashion Designer
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 77

# James

James sits in the leather chair with his legs crossed, uncrossed, then crossed again. His fingers worry at the cuff of his Comme des Garçons shirt—a piece he designed three years ago, back when his hands still knew how to create without trembling. He's fifty-one now, though he looks older. The silver at his temples has spread like spilled paint.

Two years and four months ago, his husband Marcus suffered a severe stroke while James was at his studio in SoHo. James was in a design meeting when the hospital called. He remembers the way the room tilted, how his assistant's voice sounded like it was coming through water. Marcus was thirty-eight. There had been no warning signs.

The first weeks were a blur of ICU waiting rooms and machines that beeped in rhythms that still invade James's sleep. Marcus survived, but the man who came home was fragmented—his right side weakened, his speech halting and uncertain. James learned the word "aphasia" the way other people learn their children's names. He learned it by living it every single day.

James stopped going to the studio. His partner initially understood, then gradually didn't. The spring collection went to another designer. The autumn line was cancelled. His name, once recognizable in certain circles, began to fade from the industry conversation. He tells himself he doesn't care, but his hands know better. They shake when he tries to sketch. The familiar ache of creation has become something else entirely—something that feels too much like abandonment.

At night, James lies awake while Marcus sleeps fitfully beside him. He listens to his husband's breathing, waiting for it to stop. He has learned that the heart can betray you without warning, that bodies are unreliable and terrible. Sometimes he gets up and checks Marcus's pulse at the wrist, at the neck. He knows this is irrational. He does it anyway. Three, sometimes four times a night.

The nightmares come in two varieties. In the first, James is back in that design meeting, and when he finally reaches the hospital, Marcus is already gone. In the second, Marcus is awake but completely unreachable—his eyes looking directly at James while his mouth forms words that never arrive. James wakes from these drenched and gasping, his heart performing acrobatics in his chest.

He has stopped answering calls from colleagues. The emails pile up, unanswered. His therapist suggested he might consider returning to design in some capacity, and James felt something between rage and despair. How could he sit at a desk sketching hemlines and silhouettes when Marcus struggles to form the word "water"? The guilt is suffocating—guilt that he survived intact, guilt that he resents the caregiving that has consumed his life, guilt about the guilt itself.

Marcus tries. He works with a speech therapist twice a week, and there have been small victories—words recovered, movements regained. James celebrates these moments with genuine joy that feels increasingly foreign in his own chest. But the joy never lasts long. It's always eclipsed by the knowledge of how fragile everything is, how quickly a Tuesday can become a before and after.

James's mother suggested he join a support group. He hasn't gone. He isn't sure what he would say to other people who have watched their worlds collapse. He isn't sure he knows how to be anyone other than the man he has become—vigilant, terrified, and utterly still.
